content: A systems-based approach within the healthcare system and at the community level, incorporating cascade training, support, and supervision, can be an effective strategy to enhance breastfeeding practices. This approach should include clearly defined skills, training, and supervision for counselors at various levels, as well as robust referral systems. Lactation consultants and other highly trained breastfeeding counselors can play a pivotal role in providing training and supervision to ensure the quality of care. Anticipatory breastfeeding counseling involves assessing and addressing potential and existing challenges that may impact a mother’s breastfeeding goals. This type of counseling is proactive, aiming to identify and mitigate risks, problems, or complications that could hinder optimal breastfeeding. The goal is to support mothers in achieving their individualized breastfeeding objectives, whether they are considering initiating breastfeeding or are already breastfeeding and facing challenges in continuing. In difficult or complex situations, providing positive feedback and emotional support is particularly important to bolster a mother’s confidence and self-efficacy in breastfeeding. This is especially critical in circumstances where mothers may feel overwhelmed or uncertain about their ability to breastfeed successfully. Breastfeeding counseling is a vital intervention in emergency response scenarios. It saves lives, protects child nutrition, health, and development, and benefits mothers. Emergency preparedness is essential to ensure timely, efficient, and appropriate responses. This includes training personnel likely to support mothers during emergencies and building the capacity of those delivering services. At a minimum, staff in contact with mothers and children under two years of age should be trained to address psychosocial issues, conduct nutrition screening, and provide referrals to specialized support when needed. Specialized capacity may be required to counsel mothers with heightened needs, such as those who are stressed, traumatized, or malnourished, as well as mothers of low-birth-weight infants, infants with disabilities, or those experiencing feeding difficulties. In areas where breastfeeding is the norm but practices are suboptimal, tailored interventions are necessary to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding effectively and sensitively. Breastfeeding is a cornerstone of child health, development, and survival, particularly in regions where diarrhea, pneumonia, and undernutrition are leading causes of mortality in children under five. It also reduces the risk of overweight and obesity and supports maternal health globally. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends initiating breastfeeding within the first hour after birth, exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, and continued breastfeeding alongside complementary foods until at least 24 months of age or beyond. Despite the well-documented benefits of breastfeeding, national efforts to increase exclusive and continued breastfeeding rates have generally had limited success. This is due to changing societal attitudes toward breastfeeding, challenges faced by women returning to work, and insufficient national investment in counseling and support for breastfeeding mothers. In 2017, only 41% of infants under six months globally were exclusively breastfed, and the rate of continued breastfeeding at two years was 45%. Interventions at multiple levels—structural, community, workplace, and individual—can significantly improve breastfeeding rates. Counseling and support provided in health facilities, peer-to-peer counseling, group counseling, community-based support, and infrastructural modifications to create enabling environments all contribute to higher rates of exclusive and continued breastfeeding. Guidelines on breastfeeding counseling aim to improve the quality and delivery of services to pregnant women and mothers who wish to breastfeed. These guidelines define the expected services and competencies of staff, thereby enhancing the monitoring of health system quality. They also provide evidence-based recommendations on the frequency, timing, mode, and provider of breastfeeding counseling to improve breastfeeding practices. The WHO guideline on breastfeeding counseling is intended to help member states and their partners make informed decisions about appropriate actions to achieve global health and nutrition targets. It aims to improve the quality of breastfeeding counseling among pregnant women and mothers, increase the number of infants and young children being breastfed according to WHO recommendations, and clarify the scope and expectations of quality breastfeeding counseling. The guideline also addresses the needs of specific populations, including transgender and non-binary parents, while recognizing that interventions for fathers, families, and other caregivers are not the primary focus. It emphasizes the importance of evidence-informed recommendations on the optimal timing, frequency, mode, and provider of breastfeeding counseling to improve practices. This guideline complements existing WHO tools and training materials, such as breastfeeding counseling courses, infant and young child feeding counseling courses, and the Integrated Management of Childhood Illness framework. It also aligns with operational guidance for emergency contexts and the Baby-Friendly Hospital Initiative, which promotes breastfeeding in maternity and newborn care facilities. The recommendations in this guideline are expected to inform the development of relevant nutrition and health policies and standards of care, contributing to the global effort to protect, promote, and support breastfeeding.
